Good review or bad review?

Bayes' theorem and Naïve Bayes, built by counting

Thursday 22 October 2026 · Sessions 10–12 · Prof. Shripada Hebbar

Agenda

  • Bayes' theorem
  • Naïve Bayes
  • The equations behind it
  • A sentiment classifier, by hand and in Python
  • Testing the classifier: accuracy, precision and recall

Bayes' theorem

How to update what you believe when a new clue shows up.

One of the most useful ideas in all of maths. It's about updating beliefs with evidence. We learn it by counting animals, not by memorising a formula. A practical case first, the names and the formula after.

The one idea behind all of it

Old belief

what you thought before

+ New clue

the evidence you just saw

→ New belief

updated

Bayes' theorem tells you how much the clue should change your mind.

Bayes is not a new hard formula. It is the natural act of changing your mind, by the right amount.

Meet the app

An app looks at any photo and tells you: dog or wolf?

🐺 ⚠ WOLF!

When it says that, how worried should you be?

Keep it playful. The app framing makes false alarms intuitive: everyone has had a phone app get something wrong.

How good is the app?

Photos that really are wolves 10 in 1000 (the other 990 are dogs)
Wolves it catches 90%: 9 out of 10
Dogs it wrongly calls a wolf 10%: 99 out of 990

Ask the class to predict the answer now, before we count. Most say about 90%. Write a few predictions on the board: the reveal lands harder.

The trap

The app just shouted WOLF! Is it really a wolf?

Gut feeling: "The app is 90% accurate, so probably yes."

Let's count and see.

This is the hook. Almost everyone's gut says about 90%. Hold the tension; don't reveal yet.

Count 1000 photos

Forget percentages for a moment. Picture 1000 real photos going into the app.

990 dogs

10 wolves

wolves are rare

The whole trick lives in this imbalance: 990 against 10. Keep pointing back to it.

Alarms from the 10 wolves

The app catches 90% of wolves.

90% of 10 = 9 true alarms

Correct "WOLF!" shouts, on photos that really were wolves.

So far so good: 9 correct catches. Now the twist: how many alarms come from dogs?

Alarms from the 990 dogs

The app wrongly alarms on 10% of dogs.

10% of 990 = 99 false alarms

Already far more than the 9 true ones.

This is the crux. 99 false alarms swamp the 9 true ones, only because dogs are so common.

The truth

True alarms False alarms All alarms
9 99 108

Really a wolf = 9 ÷ 108 ≈ 8%

The gut said about 90%. The count says about 8%.

Let it land. Compare with the predictions on the board. 8%, not 90%.

Why the huge gap?

  • Wolves were rare to begin with: 10 in 1000
  • Dogs are so common that 10% of them (99) is far more than all the wolves (10)
  • Doctors, juries and engineers fall into this trap: they hear "90% accurate" and forget how rare the thing was

Real-world hooks if there is time: screening for a rare disease, airport security alarms, fraud alerts.

Now everything has a name

Name Meaning Wolves
Prior the truth that never changes: how common wolves are 10/1000
Likelihood how often the clue appears when it really is a wolf 90%
Evidence how often the clue appears at all: all the alarms 108/1000
Posterior the chance it really is a wolf when the app shouts "WOLF!" 9/108 ≈ 8%

Prior and posterior are the before and after of your belief. Likelihood and evidence are what move you between them.

The formula, now that you know it

\[ P(\text{wolf} \mid \text{alarm}) = \frac{P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{wolf}) \times P(\text{wolf})}{P(\text{alarm})} \]

posterior = likelihood × prior ÷ evidence

The formula is a summary of the counting they already understand.

The formula with our numbers

\[ \begin{aligned} P(\text{alarm}) &= P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{wolf}) \times P(\text{wolf}) + P(\text{alarm} \mid \neg\text{wolf}) \times P(\neg\text{wolf}) \\ &= \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{10}{1000} + \frac{1}{10} \times \frac{990}{1000} = \frac{9}{1000} + \frac{99}{1000} = \frac{108}{1000} \end{aligned} \]

\[ P(\text{wolf} \mid \text{alarm}) = \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{10}{1000} \div \frac{108}{1000} = \frac{9}{1000} \div \frac{108}{1000} = \frac{9}{108} \]

(0.90 × 0.01) ÷ 0.108 ≈ 0.083 ≈ 8%: the same 9 out of 108.

P(alarm | wolf) = 9/10 (9 of the 10 wolves set off the alarm), P(wolf) = 10/1000, P(alarm) = 108/1000. As decimals: 0.9, 0.01, 0.108. P(alarm) is the 9 true alarms plus the 99 false ones.

Exercise: what if wolves were common?

Same app: it catches 90% of wolves and wrongly alarms on 10% of dogs. But now 500 of 1000 photos are wolves.

(a) True alarms?   (b) False alarms?   (c) Chance that an alarm is really a wolf?

(a) 90% of 500 = 450   (b) 10% of 500 = 50   (c) 450 ÷ 500 = 90%

Let them do the count themselves. The aha: the app's accuracy never changed.

Same app, different answer

Wolves rare (10 in 1000)

9 true against 99 false

8%

Wolves common (500 in 1000)

450 true against 50 false

90%

Same app, same accuracy. Only the prior changed.

Naïve Bayes

From one clue to many clues at once.

Bayes weighed one clue, the app's alarm. Now the clues are the words of a review.

A review is full of clues

5★Great price, works well, very quiet.
1★Broke after a week. Noisy and leaks.

Each word is a small clue. great leans positive, broke leans negative. How do we weigh them all together?

Ask: if a review has "great" AND "broke", is it positive or negative? That tension is what Naïve Bayes settles.

Why we can't just count whole reviews

  • With the wolves we counted every case: 10 wolves, 990 dogs
  • With reviews, a "case" is an exact mix of words, and almost every review is a new mix
  • So we use what we know about words one at a time

The obstacle is sparsity: no review repeats exactly, so counting whole reviews is impossible. Same problem as unseen word pairs in W3, only worse.

The naïve shortcut

Pretend each word is a separate clue, unrelated to the others once you know whether the review is positive or negative.

  • This is not really true. In not good, the two words only make sense together.
  • But it makes the maths simple: take one word at a time, and multiply their probabilities.

Stress that the assumption is false, but it turns an impossible count into a simple multiplication. That pretend-independence is the "naïve" in the name.

What the classifier learns, per word

Word Shows up in positive reviews Shows up in negative reviews
great 0.30 0.03
broke 0.01 0.20

One probability per word, per label: P(word | label). Plus the prior: 80% of reviews are positive.

That is all the memory it needs: one probability per word per label. Cheap, and it can be learned from little data.

Score a new review

"Great price, but it broke." Weigh both stories by multiplying.

If positive

0.8 × 0.30 × 0.01 = 0.0024

If negative

0.2 × 0.03 × 0.20 = 0.0012

  • great points to positive: 0.30 against 0.03
  • broke points to negative, even more strongly: 0.20 against 0.01
  • But 80% of reviews are positive, so positive still wins

Each number is prior × P(great | label) × P(broke | label). Words like "price" and "it" are left out here to keep the numbers short.

Turn the scores into a probability

Same move as the wolves: divide by the total.

0.0024 ÷ (0.0024 + 0.0012) ≈ 67% positive

Each word nudged the belief; Naïve Bayes multiplied the nudges.

In a real review there are dozens of words, so the two scores usually separate far more clearly.

Why Naïve Bayes works anyway

We pretend each word is a separate clue. That isn't true (not good), but the classifier still does well:

Reason What it means
It is fast To score a review, just multiply one probability per word
It learns from few reviews It needs one probability per word, P(word | label). A probability for every mix of words would need millions of reviews
Only the winner matters The scores can be a bit off. As long as the right label gets the bigger score, the answer is right

The third point is the deep one: classifying needs the bigger score, not an exact probability.

In one line

Bayes updates a belief from one clue. Naïve Bayes updates it from many clues, by pretending they don't interact, so it can just multiply.

Used in spam filters, sentiment analysis, sorting documents by topic: anywhere you classify from lots of small clues.

The equations

The same wolf story, written in symbols.

Three symbols

Symbol Read it as Example
P(A) "probability of A" P(wolf) = 0.01
P(A ∩ B) "A and B" (joint) P(wolf and alarm) = 9/1000
P(A | B) "A given B" (conditional) P(alarm | wolf) = 0.9

| means "given", ∩ means "and". Make students read them aloud: "P of A given B". Half the difficulty is reading the symbols.

Conditional probability

Once you know B happened, shrink your world to just B, and ask how much of it is also A.

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \]

Wolves: of the 108 alarms, 9 were wolves: P(wolf | alarm) = 9/108.

Dividing by P(B) throws away every outcome where B didn't happen, and rescales the rest so it adds up to 1. Draw the "shrink the world to B" picture on the board.

Joint probability: the product rule

Multiply both sides by P(B):

\[ P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) \]

"A and B" is the same as "B and A", so there are two roads to it:

\[ P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A) \]

Emphasise the symmetry. Setting the two product forms equal is the starting line of the next slide.

From the product rule to Bayes

  1. Both sides are the same joint probability: \( P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A) \)
  2. Divide both sides by P(B): \( P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)} \)
  3. That is Bayes' theorem

Nothing to memorise: Bayes is a one-step rearrangement of the definition of conditional probability. Students should be able to reproduce this.

Bayes' theorem, labelled

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)} \]

P(A | B) Posterior updated belief: what we want
P(B | A) Likelihood how well the clue fits A
P(A) Prior belief before the clue
P(B) Evidence how common the clue is overall

Where does P(B) come from?

The clue can happen two ways: from a real A, or from a not-A (¬A means "not A").

\[ P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A) + P(B \mid \neg A) \cdot P(\neg A) \]

P(alarm) = 0.90 × 0.01 + 0.10 × 0.99 = 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.108

True alarms + false alarms: the 9 + 99 = 108 out of 1000 we counted by hand.

This is the law of total probability. The bottom of Bayes' formula IS the total-alarms count from the counting method.

Put the numbers in

\[ P(\text{wolf} \mid \text{alarm}) = \frac{0.90 \times 0.01}{0.108} = \frac{0.009}{0.108} \approx 0.083 \]

About 8%, the same as 9 out of 108.

The equation and the count are the same thing.

All of it on one card

Conditional P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B)
Product rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) · P(B) = P(B | A) · P(A)
Bayes' theorem P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) ÷ P(B)
Evidence P(B) = P(B | A) · P(A) + P(B | ¬A) · P(¬A)

The same four lines are on the handout. If students can read each line aloud and say what it means, they have it.

Naïve Bayes by hand

Six tiny reviews.

Six tiny reviews

Positive

great fan
quiet and great
works well

Negative

noisy fan
broke and noisy
fan broke

Prior: 3 of the 6 are positive, so P(positive) = P(negative) = 1/2.

Count the words in each pile

Word Positive Negative
great 2 0
fan 1 2
quiet · and · works · well 1 each and: 1, the rest 0
noisy 0 2
broke 0 2
all words 7 7

From counts to a probability

\[ P(\text{word} \mid \text{positive}) = \frac{\text{count of the word in positive reviews}}{\text{all words in positive reviews}} \]

P(great | positive) = 2/7

The same "count ÷ count" as P(like | i) in W3.

Exercise: word probabilities

Word Pos Neg
great 2 0
fan 1 2
and 1 1
noisy 0 2
broke 0 2
all 7 7

(a) P(fan | negative)

(b) P(broke | negative)

(c) P(noisy | positive)

(a) 2/7   (b) 2/7   (c) 0/7 = 0: noisy never appears in a positive review

Classify "great fan but noisy"

  • but is in no training review: skip it
  • If positive: ½ × P(great | pos) × P(fan | pos) × P(noisy | pos) = ½ × 2/7 × 1/7 × 0 = 0
  • If negative: ½ × P(great | neg) × … = ½ × 0 × … = 0

Both scores are 0. The classifier can't decide.

Words the classifier never saw in training carry no information either way, so they are dropped. That is what SLP does too.

The zero problem, again

  • Same as W3: never seen is not impossible
  • One word that never appeared with a label wipes out every other clue
  • Same fix: add-one smoothing

Add-one smoothing

Pretend every word appeared once more in each pile:

\[ P(\text{word} \mid \text{label}) = \frac{\text{count of the word in that label} + 1}{\text{all words in that label} + V} \]

V = how many different words the training reviews use. Here V = 8: great, fan, quiet, and, works, well, noisy, broke.

Both piles have 7 words, so the bottom is 7 + 8 = 15 for each.

"great fan but noisy", with add-one

great fan noisy score (leaving out ½ and 1/15³)
Positive (2+1)/15 (1+1)/15 (0+1)/15 3 × 2 × 1 = 6
Negative (0+1)/15 (2+1)/15 (2+1)/15 1 × 3 × 3 = 9

P(negative) = 9 ÷ (6 + 9) = 60%

Both scores share the prior ½ and the bottom 15 × 15 × 15, so we can compare the tops. That shortcut only works because the two piles have the same size and prior; in general, compute both full scores.

Exercise: classify "quiet fan"

Word Pos Neg
quiet 1 0
fan 1 2

Add-one, V = 8, both piles have 7 words.

Positive: (1+1)/15 × (1+1)/15 → 2 × 2 = 4   Negative: (0+1)/15 × (2+1)/15 → 1 × 3 = 3

Positive, with 4 ÷ 7 ≈ 57%

Now in Python

pos_counts = Counter()                     # word -> count, in positive reviews
for text, label in train:
    if label == "pos":
        pos_counts.update(text.split())

def p_word(word, counts):                  # add-one smoothing
    return (counts[word] + 1) / (sum(counts.values()) + V)

score = prior
for word in review.split():
    if word in vocab:                      # skip words never seen in training
        score = score * p_word(word, counts)

Recap

  • From 13 reviews, the classifier learns one probability per word, per label: P(word | label)
  • A new review: prior × every word's probability, for each label; the bigger score wins
  • Without smoothing, one unseen word gives a score of 0
  • great, works and easy are the strongest positive clues; not and bad the strongest negative ones
  • a is as negative a clue as broke: the classifier only knows which pile a word turned up in

"a" being a negative clue is a good laugh, and a real point: it appears once, in "stopped working after a week". The classifier only knows what was in its 13 reviews. W04-A also shows a mistake: "easy to install but stopped working" comes out positive.

3:25 → 3:40

Break

Is it any good?

Test it on reviews it has never seen.

Training reviews and test reviews

  • Training reviews: what the classifier counts (13 in the lab)
  • Test reviews: hidden from it, used only to score it (10 in the lab)

Same as W3: a test with the practice questions proves nothing.

Accuracy

Accuracy = correct predictions ÷ all predictions

In the lab: 8 of 10 test reviews right = 80%

Is 80% good?

The do-nothing baseline

Most reviews are positive. A "classifier" that always says positive, without reading a word:

6 of the 10 test reviews are positive → 60% accuracy

Ours must beat 60%, not 0%. If 95% of reviews were positive, always positive would score 95%.

Same trap as the wolves: when one answer is rare, "always say the common answer" looks very accurate and catches nothing.

The confusion table

Treat negative as the alarm: the reviews a support team must see.

Said negative Said positive
Really negative 3 ✅ caught 1 ❌ missed
Really positive 1 ❌ false alarm 5 ✅

Accuracy = (3 + 5) ÷ 10. Always positive catches 0 of the 4 negatives.

Precision and recall

Question Lab
Precision of the reviews it flagged negative, how many really were? 3/4
Recall of the really negative reviews, how many did it flag? 3/4

Precision is the wolf question: of all the alarms, how many were real?

Precision = caught ÷ (caught + false alarms). Recall = caught ÷ (caught + missed). The always-positive baseline has recall 0, and its precision can't even be computed: it never flags anything.

W04-B · Is the classifier any good?

A support team wants every unhappy review flagged.
Can they trust our classifier?

W04-B tasks

Task What you do
1 Predict a label for each of the 10 test reviews
2 Accuracy
3 The do-nothing baseline: always say positive
4 The confusion table
5 Precision and recall for negative reviews

The classifier learns from 13 reviews and is tested on 10 new ones. Every task checks itself.

What did you find?

Tested on 10 new reviews Accuracy Negatives caught
always say positive 60% 0 of 4
Naïve Bayes, add-one 80% 3 of 4

Four questions

  1. "not bad at all" was called negative. Why?
  2. "looks great but it leaks" was called positive. Why?
  3. The support team can only read 20 reviews a day. Should they care more about precision or recall?
  4. 95% of a shop's reviews are positive. A vendor says their classifier is 94% accurate. Impressed?

Q1: "not" and "bad" only appear in negative training reviews; the classifier sees separate words, not "not bad" as a phrase. That is the naïve assumption failing. Q2: "great" is the strongest positive clue, "it" leans positive too ("love it"), "looks" and "but" are unknown, and "leaks" isn't enough against them plus the prior. Q3: with a small team, precision: every false alarm wastes one of the 20 slots. If missing an angry customer is costly (a safety issue), recall. Q4: no: always-positive scores 95%. Ask for recall on negative reviews.

What the classifier learns from its reviews 🛑

Suppose every training review is in textbook English, and a customer writes "product is too good yaar, worth it".

  • too, yaar and worth may be unknown, or lean negative
  • The review is judged mostly by the prior, or wrongly
  • A classifier is only fair to the kinds of writing it was trained on

Ask who is most likely to be misread: customers writing in Hinglish, or in a second language, or with spelling mistakes. If a company uses sentiment to decide whose complaint gets answered, those customers get worse service.

Where counting words stops working

"not bad at all"

Words, not phrases: misses the not → W8 transformers

great · excellent

Different words, same meaning: counted separately → W6 word vectors

"Great. It broke in a day."

Sarcasm: the words say positive, the writer means negative

Short check (1/2)

  1. Of 1000 customers, 100 are about to cancel their subscription. A warning system flags 80% of those 100, and also wrongly flags 10% of the other 900. A customer is flagged. What is the chance they are really about to cancel?
  2. Three tiny reviews: positive good fan · positive good price · negative bad fan.
    Without smoothing, what is P(good | pos)?
  3. Use add-one smoothing on the same three reviews. The words are good, fan, price, bad, so V = 4.
    (a) P(fan | neg)   (b) P(good | neg)

Short check (2/2)

  1. Naïve Bayes treats every word of a review as a separate clue. Give one review where this leads it to the wrong answer, and say why.
  2. 90% of a shop's reviews are positive. A classifier always answers positive. What is its accuracy, and how many unhappy customers does it find?
